summary: Defines how an application client can use credentials obtained through OAuth together with the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL). This lets protocols that use SASL, such as email protocols, access a protected resource using OAuth tokens instead of passwords.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of handing over your password, you show a special ticket that someone you trust gave you. This lets email programs use such tickets.

questions: how to use oauth with sasl
what is the sasl oauthbearer mechanism
how does oauth work with imap and smtp
what is the sasl oauth10a mechanism
subtitle: Two SASL mechanisms that let email and similar non-HTTP protocols log in with an OAuth token instead of a password.

tldr.problem: OAuth was built around HTTP, but protocols such as IMAP and SMTP authenticate through SASL. The OAuth specifications do not say how a client presents an access token to a resource server over SASL.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7628 defines the OAUTHBEARER mechanism (OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens) and the OAUTH10A mechanism (OAuth 1.0a MAC tokens). The client sends one initial response made of key/value pairs, with the token in an 'auth' key, and the server answers with success or a JSON error.
tldr.outcome: Non-HTTP applications can use OAuth tokens through SASL. Bearer tokens must travel over TLS, and the mechanisms provide no data security layer of their own.

today: RFC 7628 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA registered both OAUTHBEARER and OAUTH10A in the SASL Mechanisms registry.

sections.title: OAuth Meets SASL
sections.content:
OAuth 1.0a (RFC 5849) and OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) let a third-party application obtain limited access to a protected resource. OAuth 2.0 core covers the client's dealings with the authorization server but not how the client then uses an access token at the resource server; that is left to documents such as the bearer token specification (RFC 6750). Until this RFC, the main use cases were HTTP-based.

RFC 7628 plugs OAuth into the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL, RFC 4422), a framework for replaceable authentication mechanisms in connection-oriented protocols. That makes OAuth usable with IMAP (RFC 3501) and SMTP (RFC 5321), and the document gives examples for both.

In the OAuth 2.0 flow of steps (A) to (F), this document defines only steps (E) and (F): the client presents the access token to the resource server, and the server validates it and reports success. Discovering the authorization endpoints and registering the client are out of scope; the text points to OpenID Connect Discovery or WebFinger, and generic clients SHOULD support Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591).
sections.plainLanguage: Getting the pass from a trusted person is already solved. This document only explains how to show the pass at the door of an email server.

sections.title: The Two Mechanisms and the Exchange
sections.content:
Two SASL mechanisms are defined:

  • OAUTHBEARER: OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens as in RFC 6750.
  • OAUTH10A: OAuth 1.0a MAC tokens using the HMAC-SHA1 keyed message digest.

New access token types can be added by registering new mechanism names with IANA and citing this document. These mechanisms give no integrity or confidentiality protection after authentication, so TLS or something similar is needed for that. TLS MUST be used with OAUTHBEARER, and is RECOMMENDED for OAUTH10A.

The mechanisms are client-initiated and in lockstep. On success the client sends a valid initial response and the server reports success. On failure the server sends an error, the client MUST send one more message so the server can finish, and the server then fails the authentication. The extra message exists because some protocols and SASL implementations cannot send a message and finalize the negotiation at once.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of passes. You show it once; if the guard says no, you still have to nod back before he closes the door.

sections.title: The Initial Client Response
sections.content:
The client response is a GS2 header (RFC 5801) followed by zero or more key/value pairs, each ending with the control character %x01 (shown as ^A). The GS2 header may carry the username as the authzid. Unknown key/value pairs MUST be ignored by the server. The pairs stand in for the HTTP headers of a normal OAuth request.

  • auth (REQUIRED): what would be in the HTTP Authorization header, such as Bearer followed by the token.
  • host: the hostname the client connected to.
  • port: the destination port, as a decimal integer with no leading zeros.

For token types that use keyed message digests, such as OAuth 1.0a, the client MUST send host and port and the server MUST fail requests lacking them, because the signature base string includes a reconstructed HTTP URL. A response of just a single %x01 is valid only after a failure.

The keys mthd (default POST), path (default /), post (default empty) and qs (default empty) are reserved for future use. Their defaults must be used when signing unless explicit values are given. In the OAuth 1.0a example, the signature base string starts with POST and uses an http URL with the port included for any port other than 80.
sections.plainLanguage: The pass goes on a little form with labelled boxes: the pass itself, which building you are at, and which door. A special separator character keeps the boxes apart.

sections.title: Server Responses and Failures
sections.content:
The server fully validates the response before replying. Values in the key/value pairs that it knows from elsewhere, such as the host from configuration, MUST be checked against the client's values. The identity the mechanism reports is the identity established by the OAuth credential, but the application decides, by local access policy, whether that identity may access the resource.

On failure the server sends an error as JSON (RFC 7159) with these members:

  • status (REQUIRED): an authorization error code from the IANA OAuth Extensions Error Registry.
  • scope (OPTIONAL): a scope valid for the service. A single scope is preferred and a space-separated list is NOT RECOMMENDED because several implementations do not handle lists properly.
  • openid-configuration (OPTIONAL): an https URL of an OpenID Provider Configuration document, which lets the client find the endpoints. Clients SHOULD NOT cache one value as valid for all users or domains.

If the server gives a scope, the client MUST request scoped tokens; otherwise it SHOULD assume an unscoped token. Using the offline_access scope is RECOMMENDED so the client can ask for a refresh token, and clients are advised to use the 'iss' element to decide whether registration was already done and a refresh token can be reused.

Because SASL (Section 3.6 of RFC 4422) forbids extra data in a failed outcome, the error goes in a normal message. The client then sends a single %x01 or a SASL abort, such as the IMAP asterisk cancel. An empty auth value is one way a client can query for the needed scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If the guard says no, he hands you a note saying why and where to get the right pass. You nod back once, and then the door closes.

sections.title: Examples in IMAP and SMTP
sections.content:
The examples assume TLS; if the connection is not already TLS, STARTTLS MUST be used for bearer tokens. IMAP examples use SASL-IR (RFC 4959) to send the payload in the initial response, and IMAP requires base64 encoding (RFC 4648). Mechanism names are case insensitive.

In the IMAP bearer example the server advertises AUTH=OAUTHBEARER, the client sends AUTHENTICATE OAUTHBEARER with the encoded response, and the server says OK. The same credential works in SMTP with AUTH OAUTHBEARER, answered by 235. The decoded response there has a host, port=587 and an auth=Bearer ... pair.

The failure examples show the server sending a JSON error (in IMAP as a continuation line, in SMTP as a 334 message) and the client replying with AQ==, the base64 for 0x01, after which the server ends with NO in IMAP or 535 in SMTP. A separate IMAP example cancels with an asterisk instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are scripts of a conversation at the door: the client shows the pass, and the server either lets it in or says what is missing.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
Security properties depend on the OAuth deployment, so developers should do a threat assessment before choosing a mechanism; RFC 6819 gives guidance for OAuth 2.0. OAUTHBEARER depends on TLS at the application layer: without it the method is completely insecure, so TLS MUST be provided. OAUTH10A supports only client authentication, so server authentication must come from the layer underneath, and TLS is strongly RECOMMENDED.

Further points: an access token is not equivalent to a long-term password, so actions like changing passwords (possible in some protocols such as XMPP) should match the strength of the credential. A connection may outlast its token, and resource servers may disconnect clients as the application protocol permits. Tokens have lifetimes and can be revoked; a client MAY request a new token for each connection but SHOULD cache and reuse valid credentials.

The user identifier may contain internationalized characters, so the application must make sure it fits the protocol in use. JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) is cited as a SASL-compatible container that supports them.
sections.plainLanguage: A pass shown without a locked, private hallway can be copied by anyone watching, so the hallway (TLS) is a must. A pass is also not the same as your house key, and it can expire.

messages.note: status, and optionally scope and openid-configuration.

messages.label: Dummy response (%x01)
messages.note: Lets the server finish the exchange.
